title: The Seven Storey Mountain (1948)
hook: his memoir, named from Dante, becomes a bestseller he wrote in a cell

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gethsemani: Merton becomes a Trappist in the Kentucky hills. Your line was into the silence. Did you find your five quiet minutes? Today, the silent monk makes a lot of noise. Day two hundred seventy-five.

A man walks into a monastery to disappear. He gives up his name, his money, his career as a writer. He speaks with his hands. And then his abbot comes to him and says: I'd like you to write the story of your life. Seven years after he rang the gate bell, that story is sitting in bookstore windows. The man who came to be forgotten is about to become very hard to forget. Today: the book that made a hidden monk famous.
screen: `A MONK WHO CAME TO DISAPPEAR.` → `WRITE THE STORY OF YOUR LIFE.` → `A BESTSELLER FROM A CELL.`

segments.voice: First, the order to write. Merton had thought he'd have to give up writing to be a monk. His abbot, Dom Frederic Dunne, saw it differently, and asked him to keep going. So in the middle of the Trappist day, between the night office and the fields, Merton wrote his autobiography. Second, the title. The Seven Storey Mountain comes from Dante's Divine Comedy. In the second part of that poem, Purgatory is a great mountain with seven levels, one for each of the seven deadly sins, and souls climb it, being healed of each one on the way up to God. Merton saw his own life that way: not a straight line, but a long, hard climb out of pride and drifting, one ledge at a time. Third, the surprise. The book came out in 1948 and became a bestseller. A monk who had vowed to stay put in one monastery, and who barely spoke, suddenly had readers he would never meet. Fourth, the older Merton. Years later he said the book was too harsh about the world he'd left, too sure of itself. He didn't take it back. He just kept writing, and kept changing. The title holds that, too. A mountain isn't climbed in one step. A life of faith is a story still being told, and the teller is allowed to grow.
screen: `THE ABBOT SAYS: WRITE.` · `DANTE'S MOUNTAIN OF SEVEN LEVELS.` · `A BESTSELLER IN 1948.` · `THE STORY KEEPS GROWING.` · then, large: `ONE LEDGE AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: three lines about your journey. Have a pen or your phone's notes ready, but first just sit. Let your life so far come to mind as a climb, not a verdict. Then, after the bell, write three lines. Where you started. One ledge where something changed. Where you are now. Don't polish them. Nobody else has to read them. If you pray, you can hold the three lines up to God without explaining. The bell holds the time.
The Seven Storey Mountain. Merton's memoir from 1948, named for Dante's mountain of Purgatory, where the soul climbs one level at a time. Today's word.
Your line: the mountain is a story. Today, if you catch yourself judging your whole life by one bad day, remember it's a climb. You're on a ledge, not at the end. Day two hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Many Catholics find their way to Merton through The Seven Storey Mountain, and writing a spiritual autobiography or journal is a practice some spiritual directors suggest for noticing where God has been at work.
